'''Nicolás Yunes''' (born July 17, 1980) is an Argentinian theoretical physicist who is a professor at the [[University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign]] and the founding director of the Illinois Center for Advanced Studies of the Universe (ICASU). He is particularly interested in extreme gravity, gravitational waves, and compact binaries.

== Early life and education ==
Yunes was born in [[Buenos Aires]], [[Argentina]]. He was an undergraduate student at [[Washington University in St. Louis]], where he studied physics and graduated in 2003. Yunes moved to [[Pennsylvania State University]] for graduate studies, where he proposed gravitational waves a way to test for quantum gravity inspired features in the gravitational waves emitted by compact binaries.<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Yunes|first1=Nicolas|url=http://etda.libraries.psu.edu/theses/approved/WorldWideIndex/ETD-2847/index.html|title=At the interface: gravitational waves as tools to test quantum gravity and probe the astrophysical universe|date=2008|language=English|oclc=435913327}}</ref> During his doctoral research he worked as a science monitor at the [[LIGO Hanford Observatory]]. From 2008 to 2010, he worked as a research associate at [[Princeton University]]. In 2010, Yunes joined [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] as an Einstein Fellow.
<ref name="cxc.harvard.edu">{{Cite web|title=Einstein, Chandra, and Fermi Fellows Complete List|url=https://cxc.harvard.edu/fellows/allFellowsList.html|access-date=2022-04-01|website=Einstein Fellowship|language=en-US}}</ref>

== Research and career ==
In 2011, Yunes joined the faculty at [[Montana State University]] as an assistant professor. After being promoted to an associate professor in 2016 he stayed at [[Montana State University]] until 2019 and co-founded the eXtreme Gravity Institute, XGI, at [[Montana State University]]. He was made a professor at the [[University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign]] in 2019. Yunes studies general relativity and gravitation. He was one of the creators of the parametrized post-Einsteinian framework, a proposed formalism to test Einstein's theory of general relativity with gravitational waves.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Communications|first=Grainger Engineering Office of Marketing and|title=Nicolas Yunes|url=https://physics.illinois.edu/people/directory/profile/*|access-date=2022-01-12|website=physics.illinois.edu|language=en|archive-date=2024-09-06|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240906232012/https://physics.illinois.edu/people/directory/profile/%22%20+%20data.illinois.sections&#91;i&#93;.links&#91;j&#93;.href%20+%20%22|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Yunes extracted astrophysical information from the [[Neutron Star Interior Composition Explorer]] (NICER), a NASA payload that was installed in the [[International Space Station]], in 2017. The instrument can perform high precision measurements of [[neutron star]]s. By combining the X-ray data from NICER with gravitational wave information from advanced [[LIGO]], Yunes is able to test nuclear physics and general relativity.<ref name="montana.edu">{{Cite web|title=MSU gravitational physicist receives NASA award to explore extreme gravity and the universe|url=http://www.montana.edu/news/17032/msu-gravitational-physicist-receives-nasa-award-to-explore-extreme-gravity-and-the-universe|access-date=2022-01-12|website=Montana State University|language=en-US}}</ref>

Yunes worked on the [[European Space Agency]] [[Laser Interferometer Space Antenna]] (LISA). He is particularly interested in how effectively LISA can test general relativity with gravitational waves emitted by compact binaries. One such system is [[extreme mass ratio inspiral]]s (EMRIs), in which a small [[black hole]] orbits around a much heavier one, and gradually spirals in due to the emission of gravitational waves.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|title=MSU gravitational physicist awarded grant to test Einstein's theory using observations of colliding black holes|url=http://www.montana.edu/news/17483/msu-gravitational-physicist-awarded-grant-to-test-einstein-s-theory-using-observations-of-colliding-black-holes|access-date=2022-01-12|website=Montana State University|language=en-US}}</ref> These investigations can test whether Einstein was correct about the behaviour of gravity in extreme environments.<ref name=":0"/>

In 2020, Yunes and [[Clifford M. Will]] wrote a popular science book about gravitational waves and testing Einstein's theories of gravity.<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Will|first1=Clifford M.|title=Is Einstein still right? : black holes, gravitational waves, and the quest to verify Einstein's greatest creation|last2=Yunes|first2=Nicolas|date=23 July 2020|publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-257942-3|oclc=1181849247}}</ref> In 2022, Yunes and M. Coleman Miller wrote a physics textbook on gravitational waves with applications to nuclear physics, cosmology, astrophysics, and tests of general relativity.<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Miller|first1=M. Coleman|title=Gravitational Waves in Physics and Astrophysics: An artisan's guide|last2=Yunes|first2=Nicolas|date=December 2021|publisher=Institute of Physics |isbn=978-0-7503-3049-7|oclc=1122800550}}</ref>

== Personal life ==
Yunes was married in 2008{{citation needed|date=January 2022}} and has one daughter, born in 2014 . Yunes is the son of Zoila Lorenzo and Dr. Roberto A. Yunes, the former director of the [[Hospital Tobar García]].
